3.0.s.en: (1) The contrition of the people of God

3.0.1.en: Jeremiah feels the sufferings of his people and is crushed with them and for them, though he did not commit their sins; but as a faithful servant with a spirit of fatherhood he feels their sufferings as though they were in him. So the ruin of Jerusalem and her humiliation have come upon him, and he feels that God is the one who disciplines him and his people because of sin, using His rod, which is Babylon, to declare His severe wrath upon His people who persist in sin.

3.1.0.en: When Jerusalem was struck, she lost her dwellings and her lamps, and the dust of destruction rose and made the air dark and gloomy. All this was because of their sins, which are symbolized by darkness, for they began to walk in the darkness of sin and lost the lights of their city. All this is an expression of their loss of light, that is, of their not seeing God; so if the people began to walk in sin, God completed their walking in darkness, that is, He disciplined them by the ruin Babylon brought upon them.

3.2.0.en: The disciplining hand of God is Babylon, which did not strike them for a time but for many periods, and by all the day he means a long period, months and years, and this is because of the hardness of the heart of the people of God, for they do not return to God by repentance except through many severe disciplines.

3.2.1.en: Understand God's purposes when a tribulation comes to you, and examine yourself and repent of your sins, to protect yourself from other tribulations to come, and so that you may return to His embrace and enjoy His fatherhood and love. He disciplines you because He loves you, so He does not leave you to perish because of your sins, but disciplines you with gentleness and with severity. So do not murmur but thank Him for His love and return to Him.

3.3.0.en: Jeremiah feels, as a representative of his people, that the enemy's blows were many, so that his flesh was filled with bruises and many wounds and his appearance became worn out, and the breaking of his bones means entering into his depths and wronging his inner feelings, because the bones are hidden by the flesh. He is a symbol of Christ hanging on the cross, His blood flowing and the marks of the scourging on His back, and everyone wronged Him, even His loved ones, when they left Him and His disciple betrayed Him. What is meant is not the breaking of bones in the literal sense, for not a bone of Christ was broken, but the meaning is figurative, since these events happened to Jerusalem and Jeremiah attributes them to himself because of his feelings of fatherhood toward them and his sense of them.

3.4.0.en: Gall: a plant of extreme bitterness. Travail: that is, misery and severe pain. He depicts Babylon's siege of Jerusalem, and the ramparts and towers they built against her and around her, in bitterness and misery, for they deprived the inhabitants of Jerusalem until they were almost dying.

3.5.0.en: He likens the darkness in which ruined Jerusalem found herself to the darkness of the grave, since the corpses of her sons were scattered in the streets and the wounded were in the remains of the demolished houses, and this is the natural result of sin, namely death and the darkness of the grave.

3.6.1.en: Babylon besieged Jerusalem and prevented her people from going out until they were almost dying of hunger, and she became by this like a prisoner bound with chains who cannot move.

3.6.2.en: So too whoever is lax with sin loses his freedom, and it gains control over him and humiliates him.

3.7.0.en: Jeremiah felt the distress of his people, who cried out to God at the Babylonian attack upon them, but God refused his prayer. This is because the prayer was not a prayer of true repentance, but merely distress at Babylon's attack, which caused great distress to the people of God, and this is the discipline God desired that they might turn back from their sins. V. 9: Hewn stones: stones prepared for building with no gaps among them or an outlet for escape. Turned: blocked. It explains what Babylon did with Jerusalem when it built ramparts of hewn stone around her walls, so that if the people fled from the city from intense hunger, the ramparts besieged them and blocked their way, and the armies of Babylon seized them.

3.7.1.en: Sin hinders a person and blocks his way from righteousness and life with God.

3.8.0.en: It is known of the bear that it hides quietly to spring upon its prey, and so does the lion. Here Babylon is likened to the bear and the lion besieging Jerusalem to spring upon her and destroy her. Rather, he sees that it is God who attacks him as discipline for him.

3.8.1.en: Take care not to make God an enemy to you, and return to Him by repentance and obey His commandments.

3.9.0.en: Turned aside my ways: made them crooked, so that they lead astray whoever walks in them.

3.9.1.en: Because of the multitude of the sins of the people of God, God permitted the ways of His people to be crooked, leading to their destruction and the ruin of their cities. For their king Zedekiah allied himself with Egypt and at the same time played the hypocrite to the king of Babylon and pretended to submit to him, so the king of Babylon was angered by his hypocrisy and attacked him and crushed him.

3.9.2.en: When a person rebels against God, He abandons him and gives him over to a reprobate mind, so he walks in crooked ways that destroy him. So if you have sinned, return to God and do not persist in your snare.

3.10.0.en: It shows how cruel the Babylonian attack on Jerusalem was, like one who binds a man and stands him before him, then aims his arrows at him to pierce his body and destroy him.

3.10.1.en: God will either make you a target for His arrows or a target for His blessings and good things, according to whether you follow Him by keeping His commandments or defy Him by committing sin.

3.11.1.en: His quiver: a leather case in which the arrows are kept.

3.11.2.en: He depicts the depth of the wounds that Babylon inflicted on the people of God with arrows that pierced His people to the depths, to rid it of every hidden evil within it. The kidneys are necessary for life, so God wants them to lose their former evil life so that they may live with Him anew in purity.

3.12.0.en: All my people: he means all the peoples of the region surrounding the children of Israel.

3.12.1.en: Because of the ruin of Jerusalem, her neighbors gloated over her and mocked her. By all the day he means the continuation of the mockery.

3.13.0.en: Bitternesses: plural of bitter, meaning many tribulations.

3.13.1.en: Wormwood: a bitter and poisonous plant.

3.13.2.en: The destruction that came upon Jerusalem is a great tribulation, which he likens to a person who ate so much that he was full, that is, Jerusalem was filled with tribulation, and poisons even spread through her body, so many of her sons died.

3.14.0.en: Broken: smashed. Covered me: Jeremiah likens Jerusalem to a man whom God forced to eat gravel, so his teeth were broken. And He did not only put gravel in his mouth, but filled it and covered it with ashes, because Babylon burned Jerusalem and her streets were filled with ashes, which closed over her inhabitants, who died or fell in a swoon.

3.14.1.en: A person suffers the consequences of his sins. What he thinks is sweet in sin, he is surprised to find is like gravel that breaks his teeth, and what he thinks is joyful he finds to be ashes, after a person's energies have been burned up by evil, so nothing remains for him but ashes, regret and remorse.

3.15.0.en: From the severe distress of Jerusalem, Jeremiah feels that she has lost peace and all her former good things and has fallen into humiliation and contempt.

3.16.0.en: Despair began to creep into the heart of ruined Jerusalem before His severe discipline.

3.17.0.en: And whenever Jerusalem thought of the humiliation to which she had come and her straying from God, she felt a great bitterness like the bitterness of the plants of wormwood and gall.

3.18.0.en: And by these painful remembrances the soul of Jeremiah, or of Jerusalem, is bowed down, that is, it is broken, humbled and crushed.

3.18.2.en: 21- This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope. 22- It is of the LORD'S mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. 23- They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness. 24- The LORD is my portion, saith my soul; therefore will I hope in him. 25- The LORD is good unto them that wait for him, to the soul that seeketh him. 26- It is good that a man should both hope and quietly wait for the salvation of the LORD. 27- It is good for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth. 28- He sitteth alone and keepeth silence, because he hath borne it upon him. 29- He putteth his mouth in the dust; if so be there may be hope. 30- He giveth his cheek to him that smiteth him: he is filled full with reproach. 31- For the Lord will not cast off for ever: 32- But though he cause grief, yet will he have compassion according to the multitude of his mercies. 33- For he doth not afflict willingly nor grieve the children of men. 34- To crush under his feet all the prisoners of the earth, 35- To turn aside the right of a man before the face of the most High, 36- To subvert a man in his cause, the Lord approveth not. 37- Who is he that saith, and it cometh to pass, when the Lord commandeth it not? 38- Out of the mouth of the most High proceedeth not evil and good?

3.19.0.en: This: the sufferings by which the soul of Jeremiah was distressed for the sake of his people.

3.19.1.en: When Jeremiah recalls the sufferings through which his people are passing, he does not despair or murmur, because he hopes in God, believing that He will remove these tribulations from his people, and will comfort and support His prophet Jeremiah, and will bring his people back from captivity and glorify him.

3.20.0.en: With the simple eye Jeremiah sees the grace that he enjoys, which is that, although many of the people of God died and the rest were greatly distressed, the whole people was not consumed. The sins of the people deserve the death of all, but God's mercies preserved a remnant for His people so that they might repent, and He would bless them and compensate them for all that was past.

3.20.1.en: I wish you would thank God for the blessings you enjoy however much tribulations surround you, for by this you show your sonship to God and your clinging to Him by bearing sufferings, and as you thank Him you enjoy His care and His abundant blessings.

3.21.0.en: He declares that God's mercies and gifts are renewed for man every day: He makes His sun rise and gives His air to all, and establishes the earth and covers it with the heavens, and bridles the sea so that it does not flood the earth. He is the Controller of all and the One who cares for man, so how much He deserves thanks. God is faithful in His love and fatherhood toward man, however much he sins against Him or falls short in his relationship with Him; however much man offends and neglects his sonship to God, God remains in His fatherhood seeking the salvation of all until the end of life.

3.22.0.en: Because of the instability of the world and material things, the prophet chose the good portion, which is the love of God, and God is his portion, that is, his goal and his aim, so he runs to Him and enjoys fellowship with Him and is not disturbed over any material loss, because God compensates him. And because of man's attachment to God, whatever tribulations come upon him, his hope remains firm in God.

3.23.0.en: God's mercies are given to the one who has hope in God and faith in Him, so a person does not see God's mercy and the abundance of His love unless he believes in Him and seeks Him.

3.24.0.en: Hope requires trust in God's promises, so he waits for His kindnesses however long the tribulations continue, and remains silent however much others reproach him, because God will intervene in the end and glorify His children who are patient and strive in His way.

3.25.0.en: Yoke: a crosswise piece of wood placed on the necks of the two animals that pull agricultural implements, and it is a symbol of bearing sufferings.

3.25.1.en: Jeremiah views sufferings as necessary for forming a person's character and giving him spiritual firmness, so he calls to the ardent youth, full of vitality, not to murmur at bearing sufferings but to accept them in his youth, that he may have a strong and successful character with God and men.

3.26.0.en: He depicts the strong man's endurance of sufferings by his silence, patiently bearing them and sitting alone, set apart from all comfort, so he receives consolation and blessing in the end.

3.26.1.en: This verse and the one before it are a clear prophecy about Christ, who carried the cross while a young man, and everyone stood against Him crying out, Crucify Him, while He did not open His mouth.

3.27.0.en: When sufferings increase upon a person, he humbles himself to the ground and the dust, which is expressed here by his mouth being filled with dust, and he endures, but despair fights him, so he says, if so be there may be hope, that is, he may be fought by doubting hope, but he remains clinging to God, and He saves him in the end.

3.28.0.en: Among the hardest sufferings are psychological sufferings such as blows on the face and reproach, but a person's steadfastness in his faith is rewarded in the end by God with many glories, and here the prophecy is clear about the blows, insults and reproaches that Christ bore at His arrest and crucifixion.

3.29.0.en: Jeremiah affirms that God does not reject His children forever, but abandons them for a time that they may repent, then returns and has mercy on them and compensates them for their labors. This appeared on the cross, and Christ expressed it by His saying, "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" But after His death He rose with great power.

3.30.0.en: Although God permits the sorrow of His children for a time, He returns and has mercy on them with His many mercies.

3.31.0.en: God never intends from His heart to humiliate His children and grieve them, but He suffers for their sufferings, yet permits tribulations until they repent, then rewards them and compensates them.

3.32.0.en: Injustices may occur on earth, and a person may seize others and put them in captivity and humiliate them, which is expressed by trampling them, but God permits this for a time to discipline His children, then has mercy on them; as for the oppressor, He punishes him severely, that perhaps he may repent.

3.33.0.en: Among the well-known injustices is that a person steals another's right and accuses him falsely and punishes another who is wronged, as happened with Christ at His crucifixion though He was without sin, but God in the end removes all this, and He is watching all that happens.

3.33.1.en: Do not be troubled at the multitude of your tribulations, because your God sees everything closely and supports you until you endure, then glorifies you with glories that cannot be expressed on earth or in heaven.

3.34.0.en: The oppressor thinks that God does not see him, so he turns the facts upside down and lies in order to take away the rights of others, but God must punish him, because God is just.

3.34.1.en: If you have authority, do not use it for your own benefit and pervert justice, especially if the one before you is unable to resist you, and fear his God, because He defends him.

3.35.0.en: He declares a clear truth in the end, which is that God is the Controller of all, who permits all these tribulations for the good of His children, that they may repent and be rid of their sins and increase in spiritual strength.

3.36.0.en: By evils he means that God permits injustice, but of course does not approve of it, and He is the mover of works of good through His pious children, for it is God who permits good and evil and directs everything for the good of His children.

3.36.2.en: 39- Wherefore doth a living man complain, a man for the punishment of his sins? 40- Let us search and try our ways, and turn again to the LORD. 41- Let us lift up our heart with our hands unto God in the heavens. 42- We have transgressed and have rebelled: thou hast not pardoned. 43- Thou hast covered with anger, and persecuted us: thou hast slain, thou hast not pitied. 44- Thou hast covered thyself with a cloud, that our prayer should not pass through. 45- Thou hast made us as the offscouring and refuse in the midst of the people. 46- All our enemies have opened their mouths against us.

3.36.3.en: 47- Fear and a snare is come upon us, desolation and destruction. 48- Mine eye runneth down with rivers of water for the destruction of the daughter of my people. 49- Mine eye trickleth down, and ceaseth not, without any intermission, 50- Till the LORD look down, and behold from heaven.

3.36.4.en: 51- Mine eye affecteth mine heart because of all the daughters of my city. 52- Mine enemies chased me sore, like a bird, without cause.

3.36.5.en: 53- They have cut off my life in the dungeon, and cast a stone upon me. 54- Waters flowed over mine head; then I said, I am cut off.

3.37.0.en: Punishment: chastisement. Jeremiah marvels at his people's murmuring over the destruction that Babylon wrought in Jerusalem and Judea, and depicts Jerusalem as a man, a living human being, on whom blows fall, striking some of his members and wounding another; but sadly Jerusalem did not understand that this tribulation is discipline from God for her sins so that she may repent. This trial is a punishment from God for their sins so that she may take heed and return to Him. It was better for Jerusalem to become strong like a man in his strength and stand against her sins and abstain from them, offering true, earnest repentance.

3.38.0.en: Let us search our ways: calling ourselves to account. The prophet offers the solution, which is calling oneself to account and returning to God, then testing oneself through conduct in repentance, that a person may know the extent of his submission to God and his rejection of sin.

3.39.0.en: He completes the signs of repentance, which is that it be joined with prayer, for repentance is not only leaving sin but establishing a relationship of love with God, and he calls on his people not only to lift their hands to God but their hearts also, that is, to leave off outward, superficial worship and worship God in depth.

3.40.0.en: He affirms in the end that the reason God does not pardon His people and punishes them is their sins against God.

3.41.0.en: Covered: you wrapped yourself in a covering, which is the quilt.

3.41.1.en: When a person covers himself with the quilt, his body does not appear but only the covering, so he borrows the wrath in place of the quilt, and God is covered with it, that is, nothing appears to man except the wrath of God, and this is what happened in the destruction of Jerusalem by the hand of Babylon and the cruel killing of her sons.

3.42.0.en: Then he declares that God also covered Himself with the cloud, behind which man cannot see, that is, when God covered Himself with the cloud He became distant from man and did not accept his prayer, because there was no repentance in it but merely a request to be rid of distress.

3.43.0.en: Part of God's discipline is that He made Jerusalem appear in lowliness after her destruction in the midst of all the peoples around her, whom she had been greater than, and now she is lowlier than all because of sin.

3.44.0.en: Likewise the enemies around us mocked, and among the signs of mockery and astonishment is the opening of the mouth at seeing the destruction of Jerusalem. All this is a symbol of what happened with Christ when He bore our sins and their punishment on the cross without murmuring, and endured reproach and mockery for our redemption, for what should have come upon us He bore for us.

3.44.1.en: I wish your contemplation of Christ's redemption would produce in you constant thanks to Him and enjoyment of your new life in Him, and your readiness to bear sufferings for the sake of those around you, even if you are falsely accused in place of those around you in order to cover for them.

3.45.0.en: He makes clear the feelings of the Jews at the Babylonian attack upon them, which were fear and terror, because Babylon was cruel and killed many.

3.46.0.en: Jeremiah found nothing before him but to weep bitterly in sorrow for his stricken people. Although he knew that this was the punishment of their sins, his fatherhood stirred his inward parts to bitter weeping.

3.47.0.en: And the prophet continued in his weeping, because the Babylonian destruction went on for years, but this was necessary in order that the people might repent and return to God.

3.48.0.en: All this weeping was not despair, that is, sorrow without benefit, but supplication to God to accept the people's repentance and look upon them with an eye of tenderness and forgive them.

3.48.1.en: And here appears the role of the servant who comes forward as a representative of his people to ask God's mercies for them, considering himself to be the sinner who needs repentance, and by this he is a symbol of Christ, who did no sin and died for our salvation.

3.49.0.en: The prophet shows that his tears are not outward and superficial but flow from the heart because of the contrition and humiliation of his people, and he depicts them as daughters, that is, having no bodily strength before the cruelty of Babylon.

3.50.0.en: Here Jeremiah speaks of himself when sufferings fell upon him and he was taken captive to Babylon without having sinned, but God intervened, so they took heed and brought him back to Jerusalem according to his wish, and he here is a symbol of Christ, who died without sin and returned alive and rose from the dead.

3.51.2.en: What happened to Jerusalem in her destruction he likens to the burial of a man in the grave, for Babylon wanted to crush the Jews so that they would have no rising again after that.

3.51.3.en: And this is what the Jews did to Christ, for they were not content with torturing Him but killed Him and put Him in the tomb.

3.52.0.en: Jeremiah likens Jerusalem to a man drowning in water until his head is covered, so he perishes, and this is what happened in the destruction of Jerusalem and in the death of Christ. Therefore we Christians die with Christ by burial in the water of Baptism, then rise by His power to a new life and a new nature.

3.52.2.en: 55- I called upon thy name, O LORD, out of the low dungeon. 56- Thou hast heard my voice: hide not thine ear at my breathing, at my cry. 57- Thou drewest near in the day that I called upon thee: thou saidst, Fear not. 58- O Lord, thou hast pleaded the causes of my soul; thou hast redeemed my life. 59- O LORD, thou hast seen my wrong: judge thou my cause. 60- Thou hast seen all their vengeance and all their imaginations against me.

3.52.3.en: 61- Thou hast heard their reproach, O LORD, and all their imaginations against me; 62- The lips of those that rose up against me, and their device against me all the day.

3.52.4.en: 63- Behold their sitting down, and their rising up; I am their musick. 64- Render unto them a recompence, O LORD, according to the work of their hands.

3.52.5.en: 65- Give them sorrow of heart, thy curse unto them. 66- Persecute and destroy them in anger from under the heavens of the LORD.

3.53.0.en: The king of Judah threw Jeremiah into the dungeon, and he prayed to God, then they brought him out and delivered him, as a type of Christ who descended into Hades as a representative of us, but by the power of His divinity ascended to Paradise and the Kingdom. It is noticeable that he mentions the low dungeon, and this means there are depths, or degrees, in torment. Just as in heaven there are many mansions and degrees, so also in eternal torment, and this is because, although the punishment of sin is death, not every sin is like another, and consequently its punishment increases according to its heinousness, among the unbelieving and the unrepentant who go to Hades and eternal torment.

3.53.1.en: God loves you, and if you fall into the hardest tribulations and call upon Him, He answers you and saves you and does the impossible for you. So do not doubt, and seek Him earnestly, because He is your Father.

3.54.0.en: My breathing: the air that goes out of the nose, and by it he means its going out with a sound, that is, sighing and groaning, seeking the help of God.

3.54.1.en: The prophet declares his assurance that God hears his prayer and feels his pains and sufferings, so he continues his prayer, asking God to take heed of all his inner stored-up sufferings, which come out in sighs or appear in crying and supplication to God.

3.55.0.en: Thou drewest near: thou approached. When God heard the cry of His people or the prayer of His prophet Jeremiah, He drew near and reassured him that he need not fear.

3.56.0.en: God stood as an adversary before the enemies of His people and delivered His children from the slavery of Babylon by raising up the empire of the Medes and Persia, which brought His people back to their country, and thus the slavery of the people of God was loosed, as Christ loosed His people from the chains of sin and perdition, opening to them the door of salvation and eternal life.

3.57.0.en: Jeremiah calls God to witness the injustices that came upon him and asks Him to plead his cause, that is, to defend him and restore his glory, and this is what happened by the return from captivity and by the resurrection of the Lord of glory Jesus Christ as the firstborn among many brethren, that we also may rise in Him from every sin by repentance, and God removes from us the wars of the devil our adversary and delivers us from his hand.

3.58.0.en: Jeremiah continues his words, calling God to witness all the injustices and Babylon's vengeance on Jerusalem and Judea, that God may have compassion and remove this punishment from His children.

3.59.0.en: And Jeremiah says to God that He heard Babylon's reproaches and its imaginations of evil against Jerusalem, and he says this to move God's mercies for His poor people, as God heard the reproaches of the wicked and their torture of Christ, so He glorifies His Son and punishes the wicked.

3.60.0.en: The chiefs and people of the kingdom of Judah continued their reproach of Jeremiah and their attempt to kill him for many days, which is expressed by all the day, as the Jews did to Christ.

3.60.1.en: Do not be troubled when the wicked persist in their evil and reproach you. Do not doubt, but stand firm in your faith, for their apparent strength passes away, and God will glorify you in the end.

3.61.0.en: He asks God's help and fatherhood to look upon the plots of his enemies against him, whether in their sitting to conspire against him or their standing to take steps against him, and to deliver him from their hands after he has become the object of their mockery and their first concern, how to be rid of him; and by their musick is meant their repeated speaking evil of him and attempting to kill him. This is what happened with Jeremiah, who was a symbol of Christ in His sufferings.

3.62.0.en: Jeremiah entreats God to take vengeance on evil and punish the enemies, that perhaps they may believe in the power of God who defends His children, and he does not mean rage and vengeance on the enemies but the proclamation of God's power, His right and His authority over evil.

3.63.0.en: Blindness of heart: inability to discern.

3.63.1.en: If a person continues in his stubbornness and disobedience, God abandons him and gives him over to a reprobate mind (Rom: 28). So Jeremiah asks God to punish the enemies by abandoning them so that they lose their discernment, and when the curses come upon them they may feel their weakness, and so believe in God and live with Him.

3.64.0.en: He completes his appeal to God to discipline the enemies, that He keep pursuing their lives with wrath and destruction, to wipe out their evil from under the heavens, to purify the earth and show God alone as God of gods.

3.64.1.en: The abasement and destruction of Jerusalem
